title: Cap. IX Arg. 1 Resp.: wide difference of the two decrees; Major and its confirmation invalid
pass_a_gloss: Between these two decrees there is a wide discrimination. The former proceeds from vindicating justice, and therefore regards the final guilt of the sinner as the moving cause of the destined punishment. The latter goes forth from the liberty of God doing of his own what he wills, and therefore, as when God established to give a special benefit to some singular person, it does not thence follow that he regarded the merits of the same person as the moving cause of the foresaid beneficence, so when he established not to give that same special benefit to another, it is not thence rightly deduced that he regarded unto the final demerits of this person as unto the moving cause of this denied beneficence. We therefore say that the Major proposition, and the confirmation of the same, is invalid, because there is not a uniform consideration nor the same habit of sin as to the decree of reprobating which there is of the same as to the decree of damning. Nor does it altogether repugn, nay it best agrees, with Divine wisdom, that he be unwilling to condemn anyone except on account of the demerit of sin as antecedent and moving cause of the destined punishment, and yet will to reprobate certain ones (that is, to pass by in the preparation of special grace and the infallible ordination unto eternal life) from the mere liberty of his will, and not from an antecedent motive of final unbelief or impenitence.
pass_b_english: Between these two decrees the difference is wide. The first proceeds from vindicating justice, and so regards the sinner's final guilt as moving cause of the destined punishment. The second goes forth from God's liberty doing of his own what he wills. As when God resolves to give a special benefit to some particular person it does not follow that he regarded that person's merits as moving cause of the beneficence, so when he resolves not to give that same special benefit to another, it is not rightly deduced that he regarded that person's final demerits as moving cause of the denied beneficence. So we call the Major and its confirmation invalid: there is neither uniform consideration nor the same relation of sin to the decree of reprobating as to the decree of damning. Far from clashing with divine wisdom, it best agrees with it that God refuse to condemn anyone except for sin's demerit as antecedent moving cause of destined punishment — and yet will to reprobate some (that is, pass them by in preparing special grace and infallibly ordaining to eternal life) from mere liberty of will, not from an antecedent motive of final unbelief or impenitence.
source_text: Inter haec duo decreta latum discrimen est. Prius ex justitia vindicante procedit, ac proinde ad finalem reatum peccatoris, tanquam causam motivam supplicii destinati, respicit. Posterius ex libertate Dei de suo quod vult facientis egreditur, ac proinde, sicuti cum Deus statuit dare speciale beneficium alicui personae singulari, non inde sequitur, illum respexisse merita ejusdem personae, tanquam praedictae beneficentiae causam motivam, ita cum statuit non dare illud idem speciale beneficium alteri, non inde recte deducitur, illum ad finalia personae hujus demerita, tanquam ad causam motivam negatae hujus beneficentiae, respexisse. Majorem igitur propositionem, atque ejusdem confirmationem, invalidam esse dicimus, quia non est uniformis consideratio neque eadem habitudo peccati quoad decretum reprobandi, quae est ejusdem quoad decretum damnandi. Neque omnino repugnat, imo optime congruit, sapientiae Divinae, ut nolit quenquam condemnare nisi propter demeritum peccati tanquam causam antecedaneam et motivam supplicii destinati, et tamen velit aliquos reprobare (hoc est, in gratiae specialis praeparatione et infallibili ad vitam aeternam ordinatione praeterire) ex mera libertate suae voluntatis, et non ex antecedaneo infidelitatis aut impoenitentiae finalis motivo.
